00 - Verified genetic parameters for the NUE breeding simulation

Holstein / Red Dairy Cattle / Jersey x Denmark / Sweden / Finland / Germany

Prepared for Emmanuel Ismaila

2026-11-08

1 Purpose and rules

This file is the single source of truth for every genetic parameter used downstream (01_founders_burnin.Rmd onwards). Rules applied:

  1. A value enters the simulation only if it was read from the cited source (status VERIFIED).
  2. Values from outside the Nordic countries are allowed only from neighbouring European populations, and are labelled VERIFIED-EU (or VERIFIED-NON-EU if no European estimate was found).
  3. Where a source reports a range, the midpoint is used and the range is kept so it can be swept in sensitivity analysis. The midpoint is a modelling choice, not a published value.
  4. Anything not yet read from a primary source is PENDING and is not used until resolved.

2 Population sizes

Basis (revised 7 Nov 2026, at your request): the CFIT installation numbers reported by Lassen & Borchersen, Cattle FeedInTake (presentation “3.2 CFIT Cattle 3D cameras”, installations as of May 2026): 28,400 cows - 8,100 Red Dairy Cattle (12 farms), 8,300 Jersey (11 farms) and 12,000 Holstein (16 farms) - in 4 countries. Known allocations from the same slide: 2 RDC farms with 500 cows in Finland, 2 RDC farms with 500 cows in Sweden, 2 Holstein farms with 750 cows in Germany (country assignment of these three groups as you specified). The breed labels of the three rows (8,100 / 8,300 / 12,000) are your mapping; the slide shows the numbers without breed names. This replaces the ICAR 2026 abstract (25,614 cows; Lassen, Thomasen & Borchersen).

totals <- data.table(breed = c("RDC", "JER", "HOL"), n_cows = c(8100, 8300, 12000), n_farms = c(12, 11, 16))
n_breed <- setNames(totals$n_cows, totals$breed)[c("HOL", "RDC", "JER")]
N_total <- sum(n_breed)
stopifnot(N_total == 28400)
totals[, proportion := round(n_cows / N_total, 4)][]
##    breed n_cows n_farms proportion
## 1:   RDC   8100      12     0.2852
## 2:   JER   8300      11     0.2923
## 3:   HOL  12000      16     0.4225

Allocation to countries (your rule, 7 Nov 2026). Within each breed, the cows and farms not covered by the known allocations are split equally over the four countries, and the known cows/farms are added to their country. Germany is coded DEU (ISO 3166), the code used by every file of the pipeline; it is your GER.

countries <- c("DNK", "SWE", "FIN", "DEU")
nC <- length(countries)
known <- data.table(country = c("FIN", "SWE", "DEU"), breed = c("RDC", "RDC", "HOL"),
                    cows = c(500, 500, 750), farms = c(2, 2, 2))
alloc <- rbindlist(lapply(totals$breed, function(b) {
  k <- known[breed == b]
  rem_c <- totals[breed == b, n_cows] - sum(k$cows); rem_f <- totals[breed == b, n_farms] - sum(k$farms)
  d <- data.table(breed = b, country = countries, cows_exact = rem_c / nC, farms_exact = rem_f / nC)
  d[k, on = "country", `:=`(cows_exact = cows_exact + i.cows, farms_exact = farms_exact + i.farms)]
  d
}))
kable(dcast(alloc, country ~ breed, value.var = "cows_exact"), caption = "Cows, exact allocation (your formula)")

Rounding (your choices, 7 Nov 2026). Both use the largest-remainder (Hamilton) method: floor every cell, then give the units still missing to the cells with the largest fractional parts; ties are broken by country order DNK, SWE, FIN, DEU.

  • Cows: within each breed, so breed totals stay 8,100 / 8,300 / 12,000. Only Holstein has fractions (x.5 in every country), so DNK and SWE round up and FIN and DEU round down.
  • Farms: the reported 39 farms (12 + 11 + 16) are scaled to 40, inside the reported range of 39 farms (breed rows) to 42 herds (“42 herds in 4 countries”, same slide), by multiplying every cell by 40/39 and apportioning 40 farms over all 12 breed x country cells.
lr_round <- function(x, total, order_key) {     # largest remainder; ties by order_key
  f <- floor(x); left <- total - sum(f)
  o <- order(-(x - f), order_key)
  if (left > 0) f[o[seq_len(left)]] <- f[o[seq_len(left)]] + 1
  f
}
ckey <- match(alloc$country, countries)
alloc[, n := lr_round(cows_exact, sum(cows_exact), ckey[.I]), by = breed]
n_herds_total <- 40
alloc[, farms := lr_round(farms_exact * n_herds_total / sum(farms_exact), n_herds_total, ckey)]
split <- alloc[, .(breed, country, n, farms)]
kable(dcast(split, country ~ breed, value.var = "n")[, total := HOL + JER + RDC][], caption = "Cows per country and breed (simulated)")

The farm rounding changes the breed totals from 12 / 11 / 16 (RDC / Jersey / Holstein) to the values in the last table; scaling to 40 farms is your choice, the split follows mechanically from the rule.

2.1 Herds (blocks)

Herds are single-breed (your choice, 7 Nov 2026), as the CFIT farm counts are per breed. Each breed x country cell gets the number of herds above, and its cows are spread evenly over them. This replaces the earlier 32 mixed-breed herds (8 per country). Consequence for files 02-04: herd is nested in breed, so the herd x generation fixed effects absorb the breed effect; within-breed ranking is unaffected.

farms <- split[farms > 0, .(herd = sprintf("%s_%s_H%02d", country, breed, seq_len(farms)), n_cows_herd = n / farms),
               by = .(breed, country)]
kable(farms[, .(herds = .N, mean_cows_per_herd = round(mean(n_cows_herd))), by = .(breed, country)],
      caption = "Herds and mean herd size per breed x country")

2.2 Germany and the NAV evaluation

The NAV documentation (May 2024) describes a joint Denmark-Sweden-Finland evaluation. Germany is not part of it, so NAV’s “common genetic parameters for all countries” assumption does not cover German herds. That makes the GxE sensitivity scenario (below) more relevant for DEU than for the three NAV countries.

3.1 What these values are not

  • Protein %: the NAV document computes protein % from yield EBVs and publishes no heritability for it, so protein yield is used (your choice of Nordic equivalents).
  • Saved Feed (SF) replaces feeding rate (7 Nov 2026, your request). NAV computes Saved Feed as an index of breeding values, GEBVSF = 0.40 GEBVECM + 4.0 GEBVdBW - GEBVDMI (Stephansen et al. 2025, Interbull Bull 61:224-228), so no heritability of Saved Feed itself is published. Your formula route could not be evaluated: no paper supplied gives the genetic variances of ECM or dBW in kg, or their correlations with the other model traits. Your choice: SF’s own published values. h2 is the regression-on-expected-feed-intake metric (ReFI) of Lidauer et al. (2023), whose breeding values “equal percentages of feed saved” - Nordic Red only, applied to all breeds (flagged). DMI, ECM and body weight are not model traits (your choice); the DMI heritability of Manzanilla-Pech et al. (2023) and their DMI-BW correlation (0.58-0.65, your preferred source) are therefore no longer used.
  • MUN (updated 1 Nov 2026 from the PDF you supplied): Buitenhuis & Poulsen (2023, J Dairy Sci 106:5562-5569) estimated breed-specific heritabilities for milk urea in the Danish milk recording system: Holstein 0.22, Red 0.24, Jersey 0.18. These replace the earlier Belgian/Dutch value of 0.32 (Atashi & Hostens 2021), which is kept here only for reference. Two further findings from that paper bear on the simulation and are not yet used: herd-test-day explained 49-54% of milk urea variance (the simulation uses a generic 15% herd effect), and the authors note that MUN breeding values were not shown to reduce total urinary N excretion (citing Marshall et al. 2021).
  • CH4 (added 1 Nov 2026 at your request, from the PDF you supplied): daily methane concentration in breath from sniffers in automatic milking systems, Schneider et al. (2025). Three limitations, all flagged:
    1. the estimates are for Danish Holstein only and are applied to Red and Jersey;
    2. heritability is the midpoint of the parity groups (0.19 primiparous, 0.16 multiparous);
    3. the genetic correlations with milk and protein yield are the multiparous values, because the primiparous estimate for milk yield was not significant (0.14, SE 0.12) and the primiparous protein-yield model did not converge. The paper notes the association is likely mediated by feed intake; DMI is not a model trait (7 Nov 2026), and no CH4-Saved Feed correlation has been published. The trait is a concentration (ppm), not methane production in g/day.
  • NUE in Chen et al. is predicted from mid-infrared spectra, consistent with the decision to treat urinary N as a predicted (not measured) trait.

4 Genetic correlations

Only correlations read from a source are entered (revised 4 Nov 2026 under your rules; every candidate, its DOI and why it passed or failed is in rg_evidence.xlsx). Rules: an approximate (EBV/index) correlation only if estimated in a Nordic breed; genuine genetic correlations only from European studies; Danish over Polish, recent over old; resilience from Poppe et al. (2020, Dutch, MACE) as an explicit exception, quantile-regression version (chosen in 00b_rg_update_check.Rmd). Added 7 Nov 2026 (your rules): EU estimates from the last 5 years in HOL, RDC or JER are searched first; if none exists, an older Nordic estimate is accepted; only then does a pair stay unknown. Methane index correlations from Norwegian Red (Heringstad et al. 2026; methane g/day, not concentration) are used for the new NTM traits, flagged (your choice). The candidates searched on 7 Nov, with the reason each passed or failed, are in params/rg_candidates_7nov.csv. Traits added on 7 Nov 2026: fat yield (kept). Udder conformation, birth index, calving index, general health, claw health and youngstock survival were added and then dropped the same evening (your decision): most of their correlations with the other traits are unpublished. Unknown pairs start at 0 and are then set by the weighted bending below. Signs follow the model: high SCS, ICF and LNVAR are unfavourable, high LONG favourable; “reversed” marks a source that reports against an index where high is good, or against culling (the inverse of longevity).

traits <- h2$code
RG <- diag(length(traits)); dimnames(RG) <- list(traits, traits)
wmean <- function(v) { v <- v[!is.na(v)]; sum(n_breed[names(v)] * v) / sum(n_breed[names(v)]) }   # CFIT cows per breed; breeds without a value are left out

4.1 Weighted bending (your choice, 4 Nov 2026)

Correlations from different studies need not form a valid (positive-definite) matrix, and here they do not: with the unknown pairs at 0, the smallest eigenvalue is strongly negative. The cause is that some zeros are mathematically impossible next to published values, e.g. with rg(MY,PY) = 0.86 and rg(MY,LNVAR) = 0.64, rg(PY,LNVAR) must be at least about 0.16. Ordinary bending (used until 3 Nov) would move published values by up to 0.12. Weighted bending (Jorjani, Klei & Emanuelson 2003, J Dairy Sci 86:677-679) is used instead: each iteration moves the matrix towards its nearest positive-definite projection, with the step for each element divided by its weight - 100 for published values, 1 for unknown pairs - so the unknown pairs absorb the correction. The unknown pairs therefore end with implied values: not estimates from any study, but the values the published correlations force. This is the same logic as the bounds of Olkin (1981) for a missing correlation given two known ones, rxyrxz - sqrt((1 - rxy2)(1 - rxz2)) <= ryz <= rxyrxz + sqrt((1 - rxy2)(1 - rxz2)), which Negussie et al. (2017, J Dairy Sci 100:2433-2453) propose for filling unknown correlations of methane proxies. Every change is reported below.

wbend <- function(R, Wt, floor = 1e-3, beta = 0.1, maxit = 1e6) {   # Jorjani et al. 2003
  Wi <- 1 / Wt; diag(Wi) <- 0
  for (it in seq_len(maxit)) {
    e <- eigen(R, symmetric = TRUE)
    if (min(e$values) >= floor) break
    P <- e$vectors %*% diag(pmax(e$values, 1.5 * floor)) %*% t(e$vectors)
    R <- R - beta * (R - P) * Wi; R <- (R + t(R)) / 2; diag(R) <- 1
  }
  dimnames(R) <- dimnames(RG_input); R
}
Wt <- matrix(1, length(traits), length(traits), dimnames = dimnames(RG_input))
Wt[RG_input != 0] <- 100
RG <- if (min(ev) < 1e-3) wbend(RG_input, Wt) else RG_input
ev <- eigen(RG, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
cat("Smallest eigenvalue after weighted bending:", signif(min(ev), 3), "\n")
## Smallest eigenvalue after weighted bending: 0.001
stopifnot(min(ev) > 0)
chg <- data.table(t1 = rg_src$t1, t2 = rg_src$t2, rg_published = rg_src$rg,
                  rg_used = round(RG[cbind(rg_src$t1, rg_src$t2)], 3))[, change := rg_used - rg_published]
kable(chg, caption = "Sourced correlations before and after weighted bending")

NUE correlations (revised 1 Nov 2026, your choice): all three NUE correlations now come from one study, Tavernier et al. (2024, J Dairy Sci 107:2231-2240), NUEtot (N in milk and meat divided by N available), 1,291 grazing Irish cows. They replace Chen et al. (2021) MY-NUE 0.47 and the unsourced PY-NUE = 0 and MUN-NUE = 0. Flags: (i) grazing system, not confinement; (ii) heritability is still Chen et al. 2021 (0.13; Tavernier NUEtot 0.08), so h2 and r_g come from different populations; (iii) Chen et al. 2021 report MY (0.47) as the highest NUE correlation across 30 traits, so in that population PY-NUE is below 0.47. A high PY-NUE means selection on production alone already raises NUE.

Interpretation: 40 of 55 pairs are sourced; the other pairs carry the implied values above. Index-level results depend on these, so they are reported as consequences of the sourced correlations, not as the true genetic architecture.

5 Genotype-by-environment (country) assumption

  • Verified: the NAV yield model uses common genetic parameters for all three countries and only allows environmental (co)variances to differ between Denmark, Sweden and Finland (NAV May 2024, Section 4). NAV therefore assumes a between-country genetic correlation of ~1.
  • Verified (indirect): genetic correlations between macro-environments within Sweden were mostly > 0.9 for milk yield (Mulder et al., EAAP 2013, S14_10).
  • No published DK-SE-FI between-country genetic correlation was found.

Simulation design, therefore:

gxe_scenarios <- data.table(
  scenario = c("NAV assumption (no GxE)", "Moderate GxE (sensitivity)"),
  rg_between_countries = c(1.00, 0.90),
  status = c("matches NAV model", "scenario anchored on Mulder et al. 2013 (> 0.9 within Sweden)")
)

NAV assumption (no GxE) 1.0 matches NAV model

THI enters the GxE models as a herd-test-day covariate (reaction norm), as agreed. THI series for DK/SE/FI are not yet sourced; they will come from published meteorological records before 03_multitrait_gxe.Rmd is run.

6 Breeding goal: Nordic Total Merit (NTM) weights (added 3 Nov 2026)

The selection indices in file 04 now use the official NTM sub-index weights instead of illustrative emphases. Sources (PDFs you supplied, 3 Nov 2026):

  • NTM weights per breed: Nordic Cattle Genetic Evaluation, Economic weight of Saved feed in NTM (2026), Table 2, column “New NTM” (introduced in the May 2026 index round).
  • Milk vs protein inside the Yield sub-index: Kargo et al. 2014, J Dairy Sci 97:7879-7888, Tables 13 (RDC) and 14 (Holstein), Nordic economic values (EUR/kg) and genetic SD (kg).
  • EUR per NTM unit per cow-year: Fikse & Kargo 2020, The economic value of NTM, p. 2 (HOL 9.9, RDC 9.2, JER 8.0).

How NTM maps onto the 11 simulated traits.

  • NTM weights act on sub-indices scaled to 10 index units per genetic SD of AI bulls in the base (Kargo et al. 2014, p. 7884). File 04 standardises breeding values by the genetic SD at the end of burn-in, so a weight of 0.90 per sub-index SD is used as 0.90 per trait SD. Assumption: one sub-index SD equals one genetic SD of the simulated trait that represents it.
  • Yield = milk, protein and fat yield (fat added 7 Nov 2026), combined with the per-SD economic values above (milk volume has a negative value), scaled to unit SD using their genetic correlations, then given the Yield weight. Jersey is not in Kargo et al. 2014; the Holstein milk:protein ratio is used for Jersey (assumption).
  • Fertility, udder health, longevity are each represented by one simulated trait (ICF, SCS, LONG), although the real sub-indices combine several traits. Since 7 Nov 2026 the same holds for birth index, calving index, general health, claw health, udder conformation and youngstock survival were considered and all dropped on 7 Nov 2026 (unpublished correlations). Each had been represented by its component with the highest correlation with the NAV index (general health: other metabolic diseases, index correlation 0.83 / 0.81 / 0.88, NAV 2020 Table 41), with that component’s NAV heritability.
  • Saved Feed is simulated as its own trait, SF (7 Nov 2026), so the NTM Saved Feed weight acts on SF directly (higher = more feed saved). The production correction of DMI used until 7 Nov (genetic regression on MY and PY) is no longer needed: NAV’s Saved Feed is already defined at equal production (0.40 ECM + 4.0 dBW - DMI; Stephansen et al. 2025).
  • The other sub-indices (11 of them) are not simulated. In real NTM they take part of the selection pressure, so absolute responses here are larger than real NTM selection would give. Comparisons between indices are less affected.
  • NUE, MUN, CH4 and resilience (LNVAR) have no NTM weight. No economic value for NUE has been published (Chen et al. 2022 built their N index from desired gains, not economic values). NUE is therefore added on top of NTM at two weights you chose: 0.35 (equal to the Saved Feed weight) and 0.75.
  • MUN test (your request, 7 Nov 2026): scenario GS_NTM_NUE35_MUN adds a MUN weight of -0.35 to GS_NTM_NUE35, to re-test whether a MUN weight helps NUE under the current matrix.
  • Methane (your request, 7 Nov 2026): no economic value for methane concentration is published. The CH4 weight is chosen below from a sweep of 0 to -1 at NUE 0.35 and 0.75 (selection-index theory), at the knee of the trade-off between methane reduction and NTM lost.
build_w <- function(b, nue = 0, mun = 0, ch4 = 0) {
  k <- if (b == "JER") kargo[breed == "HOL"] else kargo[breed == b]
  a <- c(MY = k$milk_per_SD, PY = k$prot_per_SD, FY = k$fat_per_SD) / k$prot_per_SD
  sdY <- sqrt(drop(t(a) %*% RG[names(a), names(a)] %*% a))      # SD of the Yield combination (MY, PY, FY)
  W <- setNames(ntm_w[[b]], ntm_w$sub_index)
  w <- setNames(rep(0, length(traits)), traits)
  w["MY"] <- W["Yield"] * a["MY"] / sdY;  w["PY"] <- W["Yield"] * a["PY"] / sdY;  w["FY"] <- W["Yield"] * a["FY"] / sdY
  w["ICF"] <- -W["Fertility"];            w["SCS"] <- -W["Udder health"]
  w["LONG"] <- W["Longevity"];            w["SF"] <- W["Saved Feed"]
  w["NUE"] <- nue; w["MUN"] <- mun; w["CH4"] <- ch4
  w
}
resp <- function(v) drop(RG %*% v) / sqrt(drop(t(v) %*% RG %*% v))

Methane weight: sweep and knee. For NUE weight 0.35 and 0.75, the CH4 weight runs from 0 to -1 in steps of 0.05. For each step: methane reduction = CH4 response at weight 0 minus CH4 response at that weight; NTM lost = % of the NTM value of the same index without a CH4 weight (both per unit selection intensity, breeds combined with CFIT cow weights). The knee is the step furthest from the straight line joining the two ends of this curve (after scaling both axes to 0-1): before it, methane falls fast for little NTM; after it, each extra unit of methane reduction costs more NTM. Of the two NUE levels, the one whose knee buys more methane reduction per % of NTM lost is simulated (one methane scenario keeps the 20-replicate run within the time agreed).

bw <- n_breed / sum(n_breed)
sweep <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0.35, 0.75), function(nu) rbindlist(lapply(seq(0, 1, by = 0.05), function(cw) {
  rbindlist(lapply(c("HOL", "RDC", "JER"), function(b) {
    w0 <- build_w(b); r <- resp(build_w(b, nue = nu, ch4 = -cw)); r0 <- resp(build_w(b, nue = nu))
    data.table(nue = nu, ch4_weight = -cw, breed = b, CH4 = r["CH4"], CH4_0 = r0["CH4"], NUE = r["NUE"],
               NTM = 10 * sum(w0 * r), NTM_0 = 10 * sum(w0 * r0))
  }))
}))))
sw <- sweep[, .(CH4 = sum(bw[breed] * CH4), red = sum(bw[breed] * (CH4_0 - CH4)), NUE = sum(bw[breed] * NUE),
                ntm_lost_pct = sum(bw[breed] * 100 * (1 - NTM / NTM_0))), by = .(nue, ch4_weight)]
knee <- sw[, {
  x <- (ntm_lost_pct - min(ntm_lost_pct)) / diff(range(ntm_lost_pct)); y <- (red - min(red)) / diff(range(red))
  d <- abs((y[.N] - y[1]) * x - (x[.N] - x[1]) * y + x[.N] * y[1] - y[.N] * x[1]) / sqrt((y[.N] - y[1])^2 + (x[.N] - x[1])^2)
  k <- which.max(d); .(ch4_weight = ch4_weight[k], CH4_resp = CH4[k], reduction = red[k], ntm_lost_pct = ntm_lost_pct[k],
                       NUE = NUE[k], red_per_pct = red[k] / ntm_lost_pct[k])
}, by = nue]
kable(knee, digits = 3, caption = "Knee of the methane trade-off at each NUE weight (cow-weighted, per unit selection intensity)")

Expected trade-off (selection-index theory). For an index on true breeding values, the response of trait j per unit of selection intensity is (G w)j / sqrt(w’ G w), with G the genetic correlation matrix above. The NTM value of a response is 10 x sum of NTM weight x response (index units), converted to EUR per cow-year with Fikse & Kargo (2020). This ignores accuracy and the non-simulated sub-indices; file 04 gives the simulated values.

frontier <- rbindlist(lapply(c("HOL", "RDC", "JER"), function(b) {
  w0 <- build_w(b); V0 <- 10 * sum(w0 * resp(w0))
  rbindlist(lapply(seq(0, 1, by = 0.05), function(l) {
    r <- resp(build_w(b, nue = l)); V <- 10 * sum(w0 * r)
    data.table(breed = b, nue_weight = l, NUE = r["NUE"], MUN = r["MUN"], CH4 = r["CH4"], MY = r["MY"],
               PY = r["PY"], NTM_units = V, NTM_pct_of_max = 100 * V / V0,
               EUR_loss_per_cow_yr = (V0 - V) * eur_per_ntm[[b]])
  }))
}))

  ggplot2::geom_point(data = frontier[nue_weight %in% c(0, 0.35, 0.75)], size = 2.5) + ggplot2::theme_bw() +

The CH4 column shows that, with the sourced positive correlations between yield and methane concentration (Schneider et al. 2025), NTM selection alone raises methane concentration; NUE weight reduces that rise only slightly. NTM has no methane weight.

7 Sensitivity analysis: every NUE correlation scaled (your choice, 7 Nov 2026)

All NUE correlations are uncertain (one grazing Irish study plus implied values; no Nordic estimate exists). To show how much the conclusions rest on them, the burn-in and the GS_NTM and GS_NTM_NUE35 programmes are also run with every NUE correlation multiplied by s = 0 and s = 0.5 (s = 1 is the main run). With D = diag(1, …, s, …, 1) at the NUE position, the scaled matrix is Rs = D R D + (1 - s2) e e’, where e is the NUE unit vector. Both terms are positive semi-definite and the first is positive definite, so Rs is a valid correlation matrix for every s in [0, 1] without any further bending, and all non-NUE correlations are unchanged.

nue_scale <- function(R, s) {
  D <- diag(ifelse(rownames(R) == "NUE", s, 1)); Rs <- D %*% R %*% D
  Rs[cbind(which(rownames(R) == "NUE"), which(rownames(R) == "NUE"))] <- 1
  dimnames(Rs) <- dimnames(R); Rs
}
sens <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0, 0.5, 1), function(sc) {
  Rs <- nue_scale(RG, sc); stopifnot(min(eigen(Rs, only.values = TRUE)$values) > 0)
  if (sc < 1) saveRDS(Rs, sprintf("params/RG_matrix_NUEx%s.rds", sub("\\.", "", format(sc))))
  rbindlist(lapply(c("HOL", "RDC", "JER"), function(b) {
    w0 <- build_w(b); w35 <- build_w(b, nue = 0.35)
    r0 <- drop(Rs %*% w0) / sqrt(drop(t(w0) %*% Rs %*% w0)); r35 <- drop(Rs %*% w35) / sqrt(drop(t(w35) %*% Rs %*% w35))
    data.table(nue_scale = sc, breed = b, NUE_GS_NTM = r0["NUE"], NUE_GS_NTM_NUE35 = r35["NUE"],
               NTM_kept_pct = 100 * sum(w0 * r35) / sum(w0 * r0))
  }))
}))
kable(sens, digits = 3, caption = "Selection-index theory under the three NUE scalings (response per unit i, genetic SD)")

Saved Feed heritability sensitivity (your choice, 7 Nov 2026). Lidauer et al. (NAV workshop, Copenhagen, 20 Jan 2026; Finnish Nordic Red, 537 primiparous cows) estimated h2 = 0.08 for the NAV Saved Feed index itself, against 0.23 for ReFI used in the main run. The main run keeps 0.23; a sensitivity set with SF h2 = 0.08 in all breeds (everything else unchanged) is written for file 01.

h2_sf <- copy(h2)[code == "SF", `:=`(HOL = 0.08, RDC = 0.08, JER = 0.08, range_low = NA_real_, range_high = NA_real_,
  status = "SENSITIVITY (NAV Saved Feed index h2; Finnish Nordic Red, 537 cows; no SE given)",
  source = "Lidauer et al., NAV workshop Copenhagen 20 Jan 2026 (slides)")]
fwrite(h2_sf, "params/h2_SFh008.csv")
